The shortlist for team lead was due by six on Friday, and at half past four Yash was still in the pantry, stirring coffee he didn't want. It was him or Rashmi. Everyone knew it.
He thought of last month, Rashmi saying over rolls in the car park, "Honestly, Mehta sir plays favourites. I've half a mind to apply elsewhere." She'd said it only to him.
At ten past five he knocked on the manager's cabin. "Sir, just so you have the full picture," he said, voice light, "Rashmi may not be fully committed. She's been talking about leaving."
The manager's pen paused, then wrote something.
Driving home in the rain, Yash turned the radio up. It wasn't personal, he told himself. It was business. Everyone protects their own career. By the time he reached the flyover, he had almost believed it.

qa.q: When was the shortlist for team lead due?
qa.a: The shortlist was due by six on Friday.

qa.q: Why did Yash tell the manager about Rashmi's complaint?
qa.a: Yash was afraid of losing the promotion to Rashmi; fear and ambition pushed past his loyalty.

qa.q: What turning point was open to Yash in the pantry?
qa.a: Yash could have competed on his own work, or admitted his fear to someone he trusts, instead of using a private remark against Rashmi.

qa.q: How might Rashmi be affected without even knowing it yet?
qa.a: Rashmi's chances may already be damaged by words she said in trust, and she is still treating Yash as her friend.

grounding: Shows a man, afraid of being left behind for a promotion, passing on his friend's private complaint to the manager and calling it business.

At the ad agency in Bengaluru, the senior copywriter post had been open for a week. Yash and Aadhya had joined together three years ago; they still shared an auto home some nights.
On Wednesday the creative head called Yash in for an informal chat. "Between you and me, how is Aadhya handling the dairy account?"
Yash knew. She'd told him, after a late night, that she hated the account and felt out of her depth. He hesitated for maybe two seconds.
"She's said she's struggling with it, actually. Told me she hates working on it."
That evening his flatmate asked why he was so quiet. "Just office stuff," Yash said. Then, more to himself: "It's a competitive field. If I hadn't said it, she'd have done the same." He opened a game on his phone and didn't look up for an hour.

qa.q: What did the creative head ask Yash about?
qa.a: The creative head asked how Aadhya was handling the dairy account.

qa.q: What does 'she'd have done the same' suggest Yash is doing inside?
qa.a: Yash is justifying the betrayal to quiet his guilt, telling himself it was competition rather than a broken confidence.

qa.q: What could Yash still do at this stage to limit the harm?
qa.a: Yash could go back to the creative head and correct the picture, and be honest with Aadhya before she hears it elsewhere.

qa.q: What would change if Aadhya found out what Yash said?
qa.a: Aadhya would likely feel her trust had been used against her, and three years of friendship would suddenly look different.

grounding: Illustrates a man letting insecurity about a promotion override loyalty, repeating a friend's private complaint and calling it competition.

Maria, you asked me about office politics. I'll tell you something I'm not proud of. It's about the worst thing I, Naveen, ever did at work.

I was twenty-five, and Pavan was my closest friend at the firm. We'd started together, covered for each other, shared lunches for three years.

Then a team lead post opened. Just one. We both applied.

A month earlier, over beers, Pavan had told me the manager's new process was nonsense and that he was thinking of leaving. Private complaining, the kind everyone does.

The week before interviews, I found myself in the manager's cabin saying, "I'm a bit worried Pavan isn't committed. He mentioned leaving." I was frightened of being left behind, of watching him get ahead while I stayed.

I got the post. I told myself it was business, not betrayal. It took me a long time to call it by its real name.

qa.q: What post opened at the firm?
qa.a: A team lead post.

qa.q: What was Naveen afraid of when he spoke to the manager?
qa.a: He was frightened of being left behind and insecure about watching Pavan get ahead, which overrode his loyalty.

qa.q: What choice in the story could Naveen have made instead?
qa.a: He could have competed openly on his own work and kept Pavan's private complaint to himself.

qa.q: How might Pavan have felt if he found out what Naveen told the manager?
qa.a: He would likely feel betrayed and shocked, since he had trusted Naveen with a private complaint.

grounding: Naveen recalls how, afraid of being left behind for a promotion, he told the manager his friend's private complaint and called it business rather than betrayal.

The regional manager's post was announced on Monday, interviews on Wednesday, so Chinmay had two days and no time to think straight.

He and Rafiq had joined the sales team together in Nagpur six years ago. Rafiq had covered his targets the month Chinmay's father was ill.

On Tuesday evening, in the lift with the director, Chinmay heard himself say, "Rafiq's great, but he told me last month he feels the targets are unfair. I'm not sure he'd push the team."

It was true. Rafiq had said it, over tea, in confidence.

The director nodded slowly. "Good to know."

Chinmay stepped out of the lift with his heart pounding. On the drive home he rehearsed it: I didn't lie. It's business. He'd do the same.

He didn't reply to Rafiq's "All the best for tomorrow, bro 👍" that night.

qa.q: When were the interviews held?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: Why does Chinmay rehearse "It's business" on the drive home?
qa.a: He feels guilty and anxious about what he did, and is trying to convince himself it wasn't betrayal.

qa.q: What went wrong in Chinmay's choice, and what could he have done instead?
qa.a: Fear of losing the post made him pass on Rafiq's private complaint; he could have argued for himself on his own merits.

qa.q: What is it like for Rafiq, wishing Chinmay luck and getting no reply?
qa.a: Rafiq, unaware of what happened, is likely just confused or a bit let down by the silence.

grounding: Under time pressure for a promotion, Chinmay repeats Rafiq's private complaint to a director and tells himself it is business, not betrayal.

Kishore had been at the Gurugram consultancy for four years, and Farida had been his closest ally for all of them: shared cabs, shared deadlines, shared jokes about their boss.

When the senior associate post came up, Farida's name was on everyone's lips. Kishore felt something tighten in his chest every time he heard it.

On Thursday, the partner called him in for a routine chat. Near the end, Kishore said, casually, "Farida's been saying the new client is a nightmare, by the way. Might be worth knowing, if she's leading it."

Farida had said it to him alone, half joking, at eleven at night over cold pizza.

Walking back to his desk, he passed her cubicle. She waved. He waved back.

He told himself it was just information. Business. She would have done the same. But he didn't stop at her cubicle for the rest of the week.

qa.q: Where had Farida made her remark about the new client?
qa.a: To Kishore alone, at eleven at night over cold pizza.

qa.q: What does the tightening in Kishore's chest suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels insecure and afraid of being left behind as Farida's name comes up for the post.

qa.q: What could Kishore still do now?
qa.a: He could admit to Farida what he told the partner before she hears it elsewhere, and take responsibility.

qa.q: Why might Farida react so strongly if she learns about it?
qa.a: She trusted Kishore as her closest ally and said it privately, so it would feel like a betrayal, not business.

grounding: Afraid of falling behind for a promotion, Kishore passes on Farida's private remark to a partner and calls it business rather than betrayal.

"So you'll recommend me?" Jeevan asked, leaning into the manager's cabin.

"The team lead post is between you and Uday," said Mr Kulkarni. "Uday's strong."

Jeevan felt the old fear rise: another year stuck while Uday moved up. Uday, who'd covered for him during his father's surgery. Uday, who'd told him, over beer last month, that he thought Kulkarni's targets were unrealistic.

"Sir," Jeevan heard himself say, "I just think the lead should believe in the targets. Uday's said privately he thinks they're... unrealistic."

Kulkarni's eyebrows went up. "Did he."

That evening, Jeevan's flatmate asked why he was so quiet.

"Just work."

"Did something happen?"

"Nothing. It's business. Everyone looks out for themselves." He turned the TV up. He didn't want to hear the word his mind kept offering him.

qa.q: What had Uday said privately about the targets?
qa.a: Uday had said he thought Kulkarni's targets were unrealistic.

qa.q: What was Jeevan afraid of when he spoke to Mr Kulkarni?
qa.a: He was afraid of being left behind, stuck another year while Uday moved up, and that fear overrode his loyalty.

qa.q: What turning point is still available to Jeevan?
qa.a: He could go back to Kulkarni and correct himself, and tell Uday honestly what he did, rather than calling it business.

qa.q: How might Uday feel if he learns what Jeevan said?
qa.a: Uday would likely feel shocked and betrayed, since he had supported Jeevan and shared the complaint in trust.

grounding: Afraid of being left behind for a promotion, a man reveals his friend's private complaint to the manager and calls it business, not betrayal.
